speechtext: Mr. C. W. BELL (West Hamilton) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 204, to amend the Trade Mark and Design Act.

maintopic: TRADE MARK AND DESIGN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Explain.

maintopic: TRADE MARK AND DESIGN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
The object of this bill is to do away with the frequent forgeries and counterfeits of the union label and to protect both employers and employees who are operating with union label agreements against those who are not operating with such agreements, but who attach false or counterfeit labels to products.
While I am on my feet, Mr. Speaker, may I ask your guidance in one matter? It is my wish to move-and in that I hope I shall have the acquiescence of the Prime Minister-that this Bill may be advanced in the business of the House. Is it permissible for me to do that now, or must I do it after an interval?

speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
maintopic: TRADE MARK AND DESIGN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Under t'he rules an interval must elapse but, with the indulgence of the House and in view of the lateness of the presentation of the bill, the hon. gentleman might be allowed to advance the bill one step.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE MARK AND DESIGN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I think the Commissioner of Patents and Trade Marks should have an opportunity to see the measure before the government gives its consent to any rules being suspended.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

Mr. Speaker, may I ask the Minister of Customs (Mr. Boivin) whether any change is contemplated in the regulations with regard to the admission of American automobiles? As I understand it, at the present time the regulations provide that when a man comes to this country as a tourist he can bring in his car and use it for a certain length of time, but if he comes here for the purpose of looking after an investment, or perhaps making an investment, he has to place his car in a garage and not use it at all. I believe representations have been forwarded to the minister-I know I have sent some in myself-and a great many protests have been made as to the present regulations, particularly from British Columbia. It seems to me that these regulations are not reasonable,-
Order.

-and certainly they are working a hardship.
lion. GEORGE H. BOIVIN (Minister of Customs and Excise): Mr. Speaker, no change whatever has been made in the regulations admitting automobiles temporarily since I assumed charge of the Department of Customs. During the past few weeks I have received several representations from hon. members on both sides of the House pointing out cases where, in my opinion, the present regulations worked considerable hardship on Americans desiring to enter Canada. The rule so far has been that a bona fide tourist may enter his car for thirty days, and if he desires to give a bond he may enter it for six months. It has been ruled in the department, however, and regulations have been framed, to the effect that any person coming into Canada for commercial purposes, in other words, deriving any pecuniary benefit from his visit, should not use his automobile without paying the duty thereon. As I stated a moment ago, there are a few cases where this appears to me to be a hardship, but with the stress of woik in the department I have been unable so far to give due consideration to the regulations and suggest any amendment to council This, however, will be done just as soon as ihe session is over.

committee, I should like to give a little history of this item. In the fall of 1924 there was a by-election in the county of Northumberland, and one of the prices of the success of the government candidate on that occasion was this vote.

speechtext:

Mr.	HANSON:	The	contract has beenactually let and the contractor is on the ground, and this vote will have to go through. I hope the money will not be wasted. Will the minister tell me, is it still the intention to carry out the further project which involves an expenditure of $260,000? If so, I would	ask him to	pause and not proceed
further, as I believe this expenditure will not effect the end which he has in view, laudable as it may be, for this reason; I am advised by those who know the conditions on the north shore, by competent engineers, that this work will not survive the ice conditions that prevail there. Before the minister commits the department or the government to any further expenditure I would ask him to get the opinion of one of the best engineers in his department, Mr. Gray, of the city of St. John, who knows the ground thoroughly and the conditions that obtain in that part of the country, and to ask him for a report. If Mr. Gray will report that this work can survive the ice conditions in the Northumberland straits, I will withdraw my opposition to this vote or to the project. I do not wish now to be taken as opposing the project, because the government is committed to it, the contractor is on the ground, the material is all assembled and the men must be paid for their work, but I am calling the minister's attention to the larger aspect, because this, as I understand it, is only the first vote of a very considerable expenditure, involving at least $250,000 which is a very large sum of money to spend in that particular locality, with the exposed conditions that prevail there and -
with the ice conditions that will always prevail. I do not think this project will be a success. If it could be made a success, if the conditions were such that this structure could stand, I would not have very much opposition to it, because those of us who live along the coast know the exposed conditions that prevail with respect to the fishermen's business, and if at a reasonable cost we can better those conditions, I do not think any man on either side of the House would be opposed to a fair expenditure of public money for that purpose. I know something about it, I have made it my business to inquire of men competent to speak and they tell me this structure will not stand the ice conditions. Has the department investigated the project from that aspect? The question of the by-election is over and gone. This vote was designed to return the government candidate in Northumberland, but failed in that respect; therefore let us drop it and view the proposition from a business standpoint. Has the minister in his record a report with respect to the effect of the ice conditions there? My opinion is that the structure will not stand the conditions prevailing in the Northumberland straits, because it is too much exposed, and there is too great danger of the ice lifting such a structure. It will not stand for three years. That is the information given to me by an engineer whose name I will be glad to give the minister, and when he sees the name I think he will be glad to sit up and take notice.

It has been under consideration for many years, and many representations have been made as to the necessity and desirability of the work. All that the government pledged themselves to do was to erect the present structure. 1 made that very plain last year during the discussion of this item. With reference to the question of whether the construction will stand or not, I may inform my hon. friend that in the case of new work of this character involving a large expenditure, the territory and the nature of the work are dealt with by the district engineer. He submits plans and his plans and the specifications go to a board of engineers in the department. Mr. Gray is the engineer in St. John. He is on the

Supply-Public Works

But the hon.
member said that we should consult Mr. Gray.

speechtext:
Mr. Gray will

In the case of the lower St. Lawrence where we have a tremendous quantity of ice and difficult conditions, the department has Shad experience, and should be able to judge whether this work is proper or not and whether it will stand. Our report is that it will stand. The contract is a good one. It is below7 the estimated cost of the department, and I hope the work will stand as we have been told it will. There are 1,700 or 1,800 people who will be benefited by this work, and those who know the Maritime? and the conditions there to-day will surely be in sympathy with any policy calculated to assist the people who try to make their living down by the sea.

I am glad to hear the
minister's statement that Gray will be consulted. That is all to the good.
You have suggested it, and I have no objection to it.

I did not think you would, because Gray is a first-class man in whom I have great confidence, and if he puts his imprimatur on this work I think it would satisfy the public mind; at all events it would satisfy me, but perhaps that does not make much difference. There is a larger aspect however. The minister stated that the government's commitment did not go beyond the one unit, and I would ask the minister to consider this matter most carefully before making any further commitment. I agree that if the work can be done, and if it will be capable of withstanding the ice conditions, then much good may come from it. If we can do anything to improve the conditions of the fishermen on that exposed work that will not be a waste of the public money, I will not oppose it. I am not questioning the good faith of the government in this action, although we all realize the inception of this transaction.
Mr. M'acLAREN: There are two questions I wish to ask. First, does this vote cover the building of a wharf at Mispec in St. John county? The minister may remember that he received a petition from a very considerable number of fishermen at that point, pointing out that they had no protection in their occupation, coming and going out into the bay of Fundy. I think they asked for a small wharf which would act as a breakwater as well as a wharf. I feeli that this is a real need to enable the fishermen to carry on their occupation. Would the minister inform us if there is any sum in this vote which will help to meet that need? The minister shakes his head. Will he inform us then if he has this matter under consideration, and if he is prepared to look into it with a view to putting up such a small structure?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I am glad my hon. friend has mentioned this matter. It is true that there has been a petition before the department, but as my hon. friend and the members generally know, the department receives many requests for works of this character. The matter, however, will receive consideration and the work be reported on. There is nothing in the present estimates to take care of that expenditure.

I hope we shall receive some favourable indication the next time the matter is brought to the attention of the minister. The other matter I wished to bring up is that of the need of protection for the fishermen at Lomeville, in the same county. That is an important centre, and the village is devoted to fishing of a valuable character. There is a pier there, but the water is very shallow so that the fishermen cannot get in for shelter for their boats and for their lives in bad weather. It is a fishing village of considerable importance, and I hope the minister can give us some assurance that there is some item in this vote which will help to meet their needs.

I would say in
reply to my hon. friend that the reports that have been made to the department for work at this point were made subsequent to the making up of these estimates. The matter is before the engineering department, and is receiving consideration.

I might point out to the minister that I do not think there is any application for an extension of the breakwater. I think they are asking for certain repairs. I know personally that this wharf does require repairs, but what is essential is dredging, so that the boats can get to the wharf, because at present the water is so shallow that they cannot get in there.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The repairs to the structure will amount practically to a reconstruction, because they are very heavy repairs. Minor repairs could be taken care of out of the general vote, but I understand that the dredging is the larger item, and that is being investigated.

Will the minister give me some indication that he will have this matter closely followed up? I know as a matter of fact that many men imperil their lives on many occasions during the fishing season. They have not the shelter that they are fairly entitled to.

I would direct the minister's attention to the item of $8,400 for repairs to the breakwater at Cape Bald. I would point out that the expenditure in my constituency, the county of Westmorland, does not seem t.o be very large in view of the requirements there. I was in hopes that the minister might be able to announce that the work of construction of a post office at Moncton would be proceeded with this year, especially in view of the fact that the net revenue received from the post office at the city of Moncton is $331,640 per annum, Moncton standing sixth in the list of revenue producers in the whole of Canada. Tenders were called for and an estimate has been made that the post office could be constructed for $205,000, or an amount considerably less than the net revenue derived from that, post ofiice in one year. I was therefore in hopes that the work would be proceeded with this year. I should like to ask if the minister has this matter under consideration, and will have this work proceeded with as soon as possible. I do not propose at this time to discuss the expenditure that was made there in connection with the purchase of that property. It was no doubt a considerable sum over and above what the property is assessed for, but I shall not criticize that at this time.
In connection with the Cape Bald breakwater, 1 would point out to the minister that there is a need which is really deserving of as much consideration as the repairs to the breakwater if not more, and that is an ex-
[Mr. J. H. King.)
tension of the pier head at that point. The _ wharf is used largely as a shelter for small fishing boats and vessels that come in there for protection against the tides, and considerable loss of property has occurred there in the last few years. While the pier is of some service, it really requires an extension of at least 100 feet. This is a farming and fishing locality, largely inhabited by French-Acadian people, and they have their difficulties to meet with at that place. In view of the large revenue that is being turned into the federal treasury from my constituency, I would like some assurance from the minister that he will see that this pier head is extended this season, in order that these fishermen may have protection and their boats and motors given ample protection during the season. I am very glad to see this item for repairs, but I would like an assurance from the minister -that the pier head will be extended at that point in order that better protection may be afforded.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I have the advantage of personal knowledge of conditions at this point. I visited Cape Bald two years ago, and I found the breakwater in very, very bad condition. In fact, unless the necessary repairs had been made there would have been no breakwater there at all. This item of 18,400 is to complete and retain the present breakwater. I agree with my hon. friend that an extension of the pier head or front of the breakwater would be of advantage to the fishermen and give them greater shelter, but the most essential thing just now is to preserve the pier, and that is what this vote is for. The representations of my hon. friend with regard to an extension will be inquired into. I think there is something in what he says. I know the position there is very exposed, and that there are great difficulties for those who are engaged in fishing.
What improvements are contemplated at Burton court house? This place is in my constituency and I should like to get information as to what is proposed.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It is proposed to rebuild the face and outer end of each side of the wharf, from the low water level. We are doing that work in concrete. Formerly these wharves were of timber construction, but since we have taken them over we are using concrete, hoping that the work will be more of a permanent character and that there will be no need for annual repairs.

The repaiis are necessary on account of the ice?

Supply-Public Works

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
I hope the experiment will be a success. Will the work be done by tender or by day labour?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It is repair work, and the engineer's recommendation is that it be done by day labour.

If the work were done by contract it would be done just as well and cost probably less. I am not going to press the point but I make that suggestion for the minister's consideration. I think he will save money by acting on it, and get just as good a job done.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: My hon. friend knows from his own experience that when you go to repair these old structures it is veiy difficult to tell what the cost will be until you take the structures down, and as you go down you find the condition, probably a little 'better than you anticipated or somewhat worse. We find from experience that these structures can be better repaired under the control of departmental officials than they can by contract.

Will the minister inform me whether the item of $45,000 for harbours and rivers generally includes any provision for the small structure I spoke to him about at Hopewell cape, in Albert county? I do not remember whether I spoke to the minister before this estimate was made up or not. If no provision for the purpose mentioned is made in the present vote I should like to know if the minister contemplates placing an item in the supplementary estimates?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I would -take it from my hon. friend's remarks that only a small expenditure is required there?
Yes.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: If it is found by the engineering department that an expenditure is necessary for the maintenance of the wharf in question, it will come out of the vote of $45,000, which is at the disposal of the department to meet cases of the kind suggested by my hon. friend. We have no special item here for the Hopewell cape wharf.
Would the minister explain how he proposes to expend the $45,000?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
There are a few items reported by the engineering department that will be charged against this vote.
At Bathurst there will be an expenditure for wharf repairs of $300; at Bayside, $250; at Bedford, $200 and at Campbellton, $300. These are deep water wharves. At Cassils, Northumberland county, it is proposed to expend $150 on wharf repairs. For Cocagne an item is noted but the amount is not stated. There is an item for Lameque, Gloucester county, but the amount is not given. In all there are probably thirty items varying in amounts from $100 to $600.
They are all small repairs?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes. Last year the sum of $25,577 was spent for this purpose.
Is there any vote for Lorneville included in these items?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No. I have the place noted here but there is no amount set out for it.
Is there any provision for expenditure for wharf repairs at Upper Caraquet?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The item is noted but no amount is set out.

Did I understand from the minister that it is intended to proceed with the work at Hopewell cape, or that the supplementary estimates will contain a vote for the purpose? I did not quite gather whether the minister said he intended to do the work there or not.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It is not included in 'the list I have. However, I will cause inquiries to be made and if it is a work that should come within the provision of this vote, I shall be glad if the engineers will recommend it to be done. Whatever action is taken will be on their recommendation.
Is there any provision in this estimate for the wharf at Tynemouth creek, in St. John county?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No.

I wonder if some reference has not been made to it by the resident engineer at St. John. There is only a small amount of work required. I understood that some recommendation had been sent into the department regarding it but the nature of the recommendation I do not know.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I shall be glad to have inquiries made. I do not happen to have the information here at present.

Is the item of $21,000 for a wharf at Caraquet a new item, and what work is it proposed to do there?

The proposed

Close-piling?

It is a new item.

speechtext: It is a new item for repairs. The place where the work is to be done is an important fishing settlement in New Brunswick, with a population of 5,250.
This structure is the main wharf at Caraquet?

No, Mr. Chairman, not all the items. There are a few here I should like to get information about. For example Green Point, is that on the north shore?

You are looking after that constituency well.
The member for the county needs it.

Shippigan has never been
off the estimates in the last generation. I should like to ask the minister about wharf repairs at Shediac. A large portion of the vote is a re-vote. What work was done there last year and was it carried out under contract?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
This amount is
required to complete the repairs to the wharf at Shediac. The work which is under contract to F. L. Boone, consists of closing up and filling with cribwork the first four spans at the shore end, laying a gravel covering on the shore block and the first four blocks and spans, a length of 371 feet; and renewing in creosoted timber the entire floor system of the remainder of the wharf, a length of 736.5 feet. There were six tenders, the prices varying from $16,966 to $24,454. The lowest tender was accepted. It is not necessary for me to tell my hon. friend because he knows better than I do the importance of Shediac as a community and the importance of this wharf.

I would like to ask the
minister with respect to the breakwater at Ingall's Head. This has been in the estimates, I believe, for two years. At least it was in last year and it is being revoted this year. Is it the intention of the government to let the contract for this work this year?

speechtext:
Mill's Point is

I would like to call the
minister's attention to the absolute necessity of doing something at Castalia, Grand

Supply-Public Works
Manan. That is five or six miles east of Grand Harbour. I had the necessity of this impressed upon me by an experience down there last October. When the wind is blowing from the east it is absolutely necessary for the people living at Castalia to take their boats for miles down the coast in order to save them. This is not a new project; it has been before the department for many years. The expenditure was, I think, authorized at one time; indeed, if I mistake not, a small portion was built, and the matter then dropped. I do not know who is responsible for that but I would suggest that it is one of the most exposed places on the island of Grand Manan which without doubt is one of the most exposed positions along the whole bay of Fundy coast.
I would ask the minister if he would be good enough to direct his engineers on the bay of Fundy waters to look into the feasibility and the necessity of this work from the standpoint of protection to the large fishing interests at that point. They have expensive boats costing $2,000 or $3,000 and they have absolutely no harbour against easterly gales which are the prevailing winds in the fall of the year. Proprietors of fishing stands, very substantial men told me they had to send their boats for miles to a harbour further down the coast of the island; that if they did not do that they would lose their property. The Castalia people, I think, have every right to expect the building of a breakwater especially from the party to which the minister belongs. In season and out of season they have been more or less faithful supporters, sometimes greater in numbers than at others, of the Liberal party. They certainly deserve something at the hands of that party. I do not know whether that adds any weight to my plea or not, but I make it because I was convinced by the best possible evidence in the world, eye-witness evidence, in the course of a big easterly gale that detained us on the island for hours, of the necessity of something being done to protect the property of those people. The loss of one boat would wipe out the owner's savings of a life-time. It is really more necessary to do something at that point than to spend the money the minister is spending at Ingall's Head. I am not going to say anything about that. I have an opinion formed from a visit to the locality, but if that breakwater will protect property by all means let it be built if the country can afford to build it. I think however, the government would be failing in its duty if it did not do something at Castalia.
I would also like to call the attention of the minister to the necessity of extending the breakwater at North Head, Flagg's Cove. There is a good breakwater there, but it is not quite long enough. In the course of a big easterly gale with rollers coming in, the present breakwater needs another unit to protect completely shipping in that harbour. It is quite an important point where passenger steamers land!. There is not the protection that there ought to be in that harbour at low water for the fishing fleet. I do not think the expenditure would be very large. I ask the minister to be good enough to look into the matter.
There is another place there, but at the moment I cannot recall where it is. I will get the information and speak to the minister with reference to it.

I am in full accord with everything that has been said by the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) in connection with the construction of a breakwater at Castalia. For the last four years representations have been made by myself and others to have that breakwater constructed, and the minister is fully aware of the necessity for it. Last year, if I am not mistaken, he said he would look into the matter. Has any investigation been made since then?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
We have received reports and what the hon. gentleman says is true. It would be better for the people of the locality if we could do this work, but this is only one of many similar requests that come to us from time to time. It hag been the general wish to keep the estimates within bounds, and we have been trying to do so. Grand Manan is undoubtedly a great fishing community. The people there live practically on the sea. There is no doubt about the necessity for increased facilities, and I hope some time to be able to do something for these people.
Mr. HANiSON:	I do not want to enter
into any controversy on the question where work should have been begun, but I do not think it should have been undertaken first at Grand Harbour because that is a good natural harbour, as the name implies. On the other hand, the Castalia shore is the most exposed on the whole island. Grand Manan is in the teeth of the Bay of Fundy, and is exposed to every wind that blows. It is not possible to build harbours on the west side, as the minister will know if he has ever been on the north channel. But on the east side there
Supply-Public Works

should be given a population of 3,000 people some accommodation to enable them to carry on. These people devote their entire time and attention to fishing. If the government wants to retain the population of that locality two things should be done. First of all, transportation is needed to facilitate the moving of products to market. We are negotiating with the minister's colleague in this direction and he is most sympathetic. The officials of his department know just what is required and are endeavouring to fill the bill. The second requisite, which is practically the only thing which this government can give the people, is a little protection against the elements. I will not question any expenditures for the benefit of the fishermen if those expenditures are sound from the standpoint of location and if they have any merit at all, because I do think that whatever we can do for these hardy people, who take their lives in their hands every time they go on the ocean, we should certainly do, within reasonable limits, whether in Quebec, in New Brunswick or in Nova Scotia. If you do not do something along the lines I suggest you will not be able to retain that population. The people will not stay there unless they can get some encouragement. I appeal to the judgment of the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Robichaud) whether I am not right The fishing population there have been rather discouraged in recent years; prices have not been good and they have not done so well. But they are living in hopes of better days and are asking the government for sympathetic consideration. I should like to see that consideration given on both sides of the House. Fishermen as a class deserve well at our hands and we should do everything we can for them within reason.
Mr. RCBI'CHAUD: I must commend the hon. member (Mr. Hanson) on his sense of justice and fair play. Certainly something should be done for these fishermen. There are a few items in the estimates for expenditures in my constituency, but they do not cover everything that is needed. It has often been said that these items are vote-catchers, but looking over the estimates I find that quite frequently money has gone to parts of my constituency in which I did not secure a majority. I would call the attention of the minister to the urgent need for improving conditions at Lameque on the island of Ship-pigan where there is a large fleet engaged fMr. Hanson.]
exclusively in cod fishing. Last fall, a few days before the election, I was an eye-witness to a lamentable state of affairs. No fewer than seven or eight valuable fishing craft, equipped with auxiliary motor power, were crushed one against another, so that the damage was almost beyond repair. This was due to the congestion at that point. The industry has developed to such an extent that the present wharf is no longer able to cope with the great traffic. It is therefore imperative that all these structures be kept in repair and enlarged as necessity demands. I would glso direct the minister's attention to the condition at Grand Anse in my constituency where owing to the fact that large sums have been required to keep other w'orks in repair nothing has been spent in recent years, so that the *wharf is now in a deplorable condition. I am afraid it will become useless unless it is veiy soon repaired.
So far as items relating to other parts of the province are concerned, I cordially agree with what has been said by the hon. member. Every item is absolutely necessary. For example, Escuminae is bound to become one of the most important fishing points in New Brunswick. At least 360 salmon licenses are issued there annually and the fishermen are engaged in one of the most lucrative branches of the industry. We know that salmon is becoming more and more a luxury in great demand and large shipments are made from New Brunswick to the British market. They reach the Old Country in first-class condition either chilled or frozen. In this connection a word might be said about the cold storage business. We have at Montreal a cold storage plant on which we have spent some $3,000,000. I visited the plant a few years ago and was astonished to find that there was not even a trough there to receive fresh fish. I drew the attention of the manager to the fact and he admitted that it was a most serious oversight. I have heard since that accommodation has been provided for chilling and freezing fish at the Montreal plant, and I trust the same facilities will be provided at Quebec. The fishermen of the Maritime provinces need accommodation above everything else. We need facilities to market our produce-not on the Canadian market, because we have no market in Canada our population being too small, but in the markets of the world, especially of the British Isles, central Europe and the countries to the south of the equator.

wharf repairs, $1,700. Has provision also been made for repairing the wharf at Neguac?

The road leading along the
shore 'at Burnt Church needs repairing. It was protected by a log breastwork, but during a storm last season this was torn away and the road along the shore practically destroyed for several hundred feet.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Usually the roadways leading to the wharves are under provincial control. In some cases the Dominion government has assumed jurisdiction. We have no report yet from the district engineer with regard to what my hon. friend refers to. I shall be very glad to make inquiries.

I was very glad to hear the minister say he is going to consider the suggestions made by the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) with regard to the Escuminac breakwater. _ It is true the proposal has been before the country for a number of years, but like many other proposals, although it was thought to be a good thing at the time it is not now considered to be quite so good. The fishermen down there are very doubtful with respect to it. In the first place, it is going to require very much more money. Then the distance of 310 feet will not afford much protection; certainly this will have to be extended. The fishermen say that if the gulley was dredged out they would not require the breakwater at all. It is a very rough place to build the breakwater, the bottom being of shaley rock, and it is very difficult to make fastenings hold in it. Then again, very few fishermen can get in there, and in case of a storm it is much safer and easier for them to run into the mouth of the river behind Fox island or Portage island for shelter. I would be very sorry to interfere with the expenditure of money in my county-I should like to see this money spent, and a great deal more-but I think we ought to get the fullest value in return. Our people down there feel that it would be of greater benefit to both the farmers and the fishermen, if this money and some more were put into the construction of a railway to connect with the railway at Loggieville. At present auto trucks are used to transport the fish from that section of the country up to the railway. I hope the minister will give
the suggestion serious consideration before he starts in with the breakwater. As I say, I should like to see the money spent there, but at the same time I should like to see full value secured for the expenditure. I congratulate the member for Gloucester (Mr. Robichaud), he certainly deserves very great credit, for a little over a third of the whole estimate for New Brunswick is going into his county.

My hon. friend is
getting more for his county than I am for mine.
What is the nature of the proposed expenditure of $2,700 for wharf repairs at White Head? Does it include dredging? This is necessary around the wharf.

I find that in 1910 it was recommended by Mr. Loggie, later by the Hon. J. D. Hazen in 1913, and so on down to last year, when we were advised that this work would give considerable protection to the fishermen. That is not the question. Is the minister's memory sufficiently good to enable him to tell us whether or not it was represented to the House in the first place that the whole of the cost would be $100,000 at most?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No.

Anyway, how
is my hon. friend getting on with the governmental policy of shipping all of our raw resources out as quickly and as cheaply as possible? Will this American firm that came from Erie, Pennsylvania, be helped to export our raw materials, which they have been able to collect, in the chepaest way possible and over the wharf we built? When will they be able to complete that programme?

My hon. friend
knows that Price Brothers are operating there now, cutting 15,000,000 feet of lumber a year and shipping it directly from the port. It would be only fair for him to make that statement.

My hon. friend is labouring under a strange delusion if he thinks that there is any analogy between an American manufacturer operating in Canada and one operating in the United States. He seems to think it is immaterial whether the workmen employed in manufacturing our own raw material are engaged in the United States or in Canada. The mills of Price Brothers are here and they manufacture here, but I understand that the Hammermill plant is in the United States. I was asking the minister a simple question. I want to know what progress the government has made in its policy of making easy the demolition of our natural resources and the shipment of them to facilitate the work of American manufacturers?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The hon. gentleman has not put the matter fairly. Matane is one of the harbours on the north shore-
The south shore.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The south shore.
If the minister's story is no more correct than his geography-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
There is no mistake about the story. Price Brothers have been carrying on business for years and they were anxious for the purposes of development to have this work done. It is true that we were requested to provide the facilities but we considered it only fair that the people

Supply-Public Works
who were so largely interested should do something in the way of co-operation. This is the first time the Public Works department has got $100,000 from any firm to build any structure.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I do not know about
that, but it is the first time certainly that the government has ever put up $165,000 to help an American firm take business from our own railway and ship our own raw material out of the country to be manufactured in the United States. This enterprise takes all the belts, cups, records and everything else as a precedent. It is a political wharf from the beginning, but it is one of the most insane political ventures I know of. The American firm came over to get our pulpwood, desiring to have it manufactured in Erie. Of course they did not want to pay freight so they persuaded the government to dig into the treasury and build a wharf to enable them to ship the material by water, thus avoiding freight charges. And they are enabled to get our raw material out all the faster and cheaper as a result of accommodation afforded them by the government, out of the money of the Canadian people. Of course there were other objects that were served incidentally. I understand that the son of the late member for the distridt was made inspector. I do not know wh'at the government is doing now for the late member himself, I have not heard. Has he received a job on the wharf since he lost the nomination or the election? He lost something, I do not know what it was, but I should not be surprised if the wharf lost him the nomination. Anyway, has the government taken care of him, or will it put him on the Indian service like Mr. Sexsmith? What is to be done about Pelletier?
He is not provided for in the Public Works estimate.

As the representative for Matane I know this wharf very well, and I can assure the committee that it serves not only the Hammermill Company and Price Brothers but various schooners that ply between Matane and Quebec and Gaspe. It also accommodates the people on the north shore; the Ontario Pulp and Paper Company and other concerns operating timber limits make use of it, and it provides a shelter for vessels coming from Quebec or going up from Gaspe in stormy weather. Most of the money has been spent and this vote is necessary to complete the work. It is one of the most important public works which the department has carried out in my constituency, and I have no doubt that the public will approve of the expenditure.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I congratulate the hon. member (Mr. Dionne) on what, so far as I can recall, is his maiden speech in the House. Certainly it was couched in splendid English.
I am sorry, however, that the hon. gentleman could not exhibit his powers in a nobler cause. It is true that any wharf, wherever it may be built, will serve purposes subsidiary to the main object for which it was built. I do not doubt some boats sail across the river but, as everybody knows, they could not be in any real sense commercial boats. These boats make use of the wharf, and I suppose boats could be found to make use of any wharf in the world. And if a boat were caught in a storm it would naturally pull in to the wharf. But that would be true no matter where you built a wharf. I suppose also this wharf serves as a shelter and shade for the fishes in the district. All these things can be said of this particular wharf. But the great central fact remains that it was built to help the Hammermill Paper Company take our raw material out of Canada to their mill in Erie. That was the purpose for which it was built, as everyone knows, and because on the completion of it other people made use of it is no justification for spending such a large sum of money on a structure the main purpose of which is injurious to the country and even to the district from which the hon. member comes. The main purpose served ,by that wharf is harmful to the district, even though certain people for whom the wharf was not originally intended are accommodated. If we are bound to have our pulpwood shipped out of the country, if we are bound to furnish material for American workmen, for goodness' sake let the people who want to profit thereby provide their own facilities. After they do put them up there will be shelter all right for all sorts of men and animals in that district; it will serve the purpose just as well. But there is no reason why we ought to put up money to help get our pulpwood out and reduce the revenues of the National Railways. I have not got an answer yet to what was done about young Pelletier. Is he still on the job?
He has got no job.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
My right hon.
friend is hardly fair. He would lead the House to believe that the Hammermill com-

Supply-Public Works

pany alone will receive the benefit of this construction. That is not so. There are some 3,500 inhabitants at Matane who will participate. There has been a harbour there for years.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I know.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
This vote is to
provide proper facilities.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Where is it built in relation to the Hammermill company? Right at the company's plant?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It is not for the Hammermill company alone. Price Brothers manufacture fifteen million feet of lumber there. Outside of the two large concerns there are five or six lumber mills with a total output of 10,000,000 feet. That is an industry in itself. These smaller mills may not count in the mind of my right hon. friend, but they are there and they require better facilities. The Hammermill company have put up $100,000 and we have put up $165,000. The whole community will have better facilities. The Hammermill company are operating as other people are in this country who own their own lands. If leasehold they could not export, but they have bought these lands, and therefore have the right to export. There is undoubtedly necessity for this development, and personally I think we have made a pretty good arrangement in getting $100,000 from the Hammermill company for the benefits they will receive.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The minister has dodged the question as to whether this wharf is not right beside the Hammermill company's plant.

Assuming it is, and the
public are using it, what difference does it make, particularly when the Hammermill company are putting up $100,000?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The use the public will
make of it is trifling. The public got on all right before.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: This work is not tributary to the Hammermill company any more than it is to Price Brothers; as a matter of fact it is nearer Price Brothers' plant.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I had a deputation come to me about it. They told me the work is right beside the Hammermill plant.	The
harbour was allowed to go to pieces. I suppose it was put in shape before the election?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
As I explained
to the House, an ice shove disturbed the works, which I believe have been repaired.
When is the work going to be finished?	.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: This year.
My hon. friend's expectation is that export can go on this year?
The minister has not yet made it clear to me. He says the cost of the work is $165,000 and that we spent $84,000 last year. If that is the case, the $55,000 now requested will not pay the bill.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I advised the
House that the total estimated expenditure was $265,000-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
-of which the
Hammermill company will pay $100,OOO. It is necessary for us to vote the $265,000.

Where are we
voting the $265,000?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: We vote it from year to .year. This item has been before the House for the last three years.
Then all I can say is my hon. friend is getting light as he goes along.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I am trying to
give light.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman,
there was no misunderstanding because I read the statement which I have before me. Perhaps my hon. friend did not hear me correctly. The estimated total cost is $265,000. There is a contribution from the Hammermill company of $100,000, and the estimated cost to the department is $165,000. That is the information I conveyed.
I am very glad to hear that. I really do my best to follow what my hon. friend says, but he has an uncomfortable way of admiring his toes when he is talking, and I confess I did not get all he said.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I am sorry.

Item agreed to.

Nicolet-repairs to jetty, $17,400.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: This is for repairs. The work is under contract to Messrs. Page <fe Page.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: What is the total cost?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The amount of
the contract is $15,750. We had tenders from four competing firms, the lowest was that of Page & Page, $15,750, and the highest $19,016.
There was a vote of $13,300 last year. You did not go on with it, did you?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No, it is a revote. Only $412.64 was spent last year.
When was the contract let?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The order in council was passed January 21, 1926.
When was the contract advertised?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: November or December-it would be late.

I doubt that very much. Does my hon. friend say he issued any advertisements after the election until that time? The country understood the government was not functioning. The government pretended it was not functioning.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I am advised that tenders were due October 21 last. No contract was let until January.
That sounds very much more reasonable. I was quite sure those advertisements were issued before the election; we know it now.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Norton Creek-dredging, $5,000.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: What is the idea of dredging a creek?

To make it
deeper.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: This is to continue certain excavations that were started in 1912 and 1913. They were suspended during the war. About 17,000 cubic yards will be removed.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Where is it?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: In the district of Chateauguay-Huntingdon.
Is it by contract?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No, day labour.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Does the member for the riding prefer the day labour method?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I am not so sure.

I would point out to my hon. friend that this is a case where there ought to be a contract, the amount being $5,000. Or was it considered more convenient before the election to have a lot of people employed by day labour? Would that be it?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
This construction was undertaken away back in 1912-13. I find that at that time the work done by day labour amounted to $4,470. In 1913-14, 4,200 cubic yards were excavated at a cost of $4,491.78, done by day labour. In 1914-15, 5,972 cubic yards were excavated at a cost of $4,9S7.42, the total expenditure being $13,949.49.
It was considered advisable at that time that the work should be done by day labour, and the same plan is followed this year.

You take it by
vote, so much a year. I do not observe that we got up to $5,000 any time during that period. Am I right?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I have not the estimates for all the period, but we find that in the year 1914 it was $4,987.42, pretty near the mark. The chances are that we will not spend the full $5,000 this year, but that is the amount asked.
I was asking as to what we did with it last year. How much dredging was done last year, and how many men were employed last September and October?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: My hon. friend is wrong about that.

My hon. friend delights in ancient history to-day, telling us what happened in 1912-13, but he fails to give details of what happened in the year 1925, under his administration. What did he do in September and October last year under this vote?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I think the best justification for this expenditure in the minds of my hon. friends would be that they undertook the work when they were in office. I think that would satisfy them, and that is * why I referred to it.
Oh no.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
And the fact that it was done by day labour would indicate that the government were following the practice which the engineers thought was good practice. There was no expenditure last year.

Nothing was
done last year?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No.
Are you sure about that?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
What an awful oversight. How did that happen? I do not think you have been properly advised? Are you sure you did not get a lot of good work in under the general vote?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No, we did not.
Do you think that because we dredged one year we must always go on dredging? How is it necessary that dredging done one year must be done the next year? My hon. friend goes back to 1912-

speechtext: The work was not completed.

Is this a silting stream ?

speechtext: No.

You know that in every
doubtful county there is dredging during an election.
My hon. friend is right.
You ought to know, as well as the hon. member for South Winnipeg (Mr. Rogers).

Item agreed to.
Notre Dame de Pierreville-wharf, $13,500.
This is a revote. It was in the estimates last year and nothing was done. Can the minister give us any explanation why nothing was done last year?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It is one of those items that we have from year'to year. Plans were prepared and1 tenders were called for, but the season had passed and it went over . till the next year, and we are revotiing the money.
What are the details?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
An order in
council was passed on the 21st October 1925, accepting the tender of J. J. Collins of Trois Rivieres. There were seven tenders and the figures vary from $9,385 to $18,080.53.

This was also
in the supplementaries of last year.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It would be.

You are asking for $500
more this year than last year. Have you an estimate of the cost of the work down as fine as that?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That is the
estimated cost, *$13,500.

Here is another illustration of how things can be done. This item stands out as a startling corroboration of the statement of the hon. member for Cartier. He shows that he is not only frank but veracious-not voracious but veracious. We have a beautiful illustration of what happened in connection with the matter last year. We have this vote brought down in the supplementaries, and this matter is arranged carefully, properly and regularly. They are pretty clever in the Public Works department, and in the ordinary course it is dangled before the electors that this project is going on, and the contract let, and when the campaign is roaring the fiercest, and the war with Turkey is imminent, we see in all the local papers the statement that this work is to be given out and labourers will be employed. We have the contract let on the 21st of October, and then of course it takes a little time before anything can be done. All the good political work, if my hon. friend will look at it, is accomplished, and we have the vote again this year.
Do you suggest that during election no work could be done at all? You know the maxim that the King's government must go on.

You miss the
point: You say the work must go on, but the King's government was at a standstill for some period. It has been resuscitated I admit, but we will not go into the operation of resuscitation. There was, however, a time of suspended animation. You will notice that while everything was done to favourably impress the voters as to what was going to be done, not one single thing was done. Contracts were advertised and let but nothing else was done.

The minister did not give us the necessity for it.

Petite Riviere Romaine-to recoup the Paint River Oxide Company for repairing public wharf, $7;525.08.
Would the minister explain this item?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: This is required to reimburse the Paint River Oxide Company who performed urgent repairs to a public wharf under the instructions and supervision of this department. The vouchers and the work have been duly certified by the district engineer.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: What riding is this in?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It was found that there had been settlement of the ballast and that the wharf was not usable. The company that was using the wharf suggested that they do the repairing.
This has nothing to do with the peroxide people we hear so much about.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
No, this is a red mixture. It was necessary to make these repairs in order that the company could carry on their work. The work was done under our direction, and this is to recoup them.
Mr. STEWART (Leeds) When was this work done?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: In the latter part of the summer, about August.
When was it completed?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I have not the date here, but I imagine within a few weeks.

I wonder if the minister has an order in council dealing with this matter? Is this a new precedent altogether? Personally, I cannot ever recollect this course of action having been followed before. Is this making history, and if it is making history, in what riding were we making history?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Thi3 is in the riding of Charlevoix-Saguenay.
That is the chief whip's riding.
I never asked for this work, and I know nothing about it.

How impossible!
I wonder how on earth it was that the chief whip had nothing to do with this. If this has taken place under the chief whip's nose without his knowing anything about it, I think we ought to strike the item out. I am suife the chief whip is against it.
Anything that has been done in this matter, was done before I came to be the member for the district. I have not had an opportunity even to see the place yet. I have never seen this wharf at all.
Apparently the chief whip can plead a successful alibi, and we will accept it. Who was the sitting member that got this new history made?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Representations were made to us that the wharf had settled, and that they could not make shipments over it. It was essential that the work should be done, and the company did the work, and we are now proposing to recoup them. The work was done under our supervision. There is nothing very unusual about it.

I do not think my hon. friend is doing himself justice when he says there is nothing unusual in this. We have hundreds of items in these estimates, Mr. Chairman, but you will search in vain to find another one like this, and if you go through the estimates of last year you will not find another one like it. Will my hon. friend tell me, on sober reflection, that this is being done in the usual way? If he will, I am content to take his answer, but I do not think he had better.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I did not say it
was usual. This work was unexpected.
My hon. friend said that this was the usual course.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I said that there was nothing very unusual about it.
It is only partly unusual ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
It was a work of
necessity.

Supply-Public Works

Will my hon.
friend tell me now who the happy member is that gets this new departure?

As I said before, I have not asked for this, and I do not know anything about it. It is in what was known as the riding of Chicoutimi-Saguenay and the sitting member for that riding was Doctor Savard. The riding is now Charlevoix-Saguenay.

I would not
seek to charge my hon. friend with any complicity in this at all. I am very glad to know that he is clear this time. Is this our property or the property of the company?
It is our property.

What was the
date of this order in council which permitted this company to make repairs upon our property, and under what terms were they allowed to do that work? Will my hon. friend read the order in council? It would lot 'be long.
( Mr. KING (Kootenay): I understand that there is no order in council regarding these repairs. It was reported to us that in order that they could make their shipments, repairs to the wharf were necessary, and' the company undertook to make the repairs and take their chance of having parliament pass an appropriation.

Now we are
getting at the real situation. There was no order in council. There is no authority for this work. The simple position is that a company that wanted this work done for the purpose of looking after its business spends this money, and my hon. friend now proposes to recoup them. It is a very nice way, Mr. Chairman, for the department to spend money without any permission of parliament. It is a very serious back-door method of carrying on the country's business. If that were done generally, we could make up all our estimates ex post facto, and all we would need to do then would be to vote the money to cover expenditures on works that the ministry had permitted their friends to do, work done by favoured companies of the ministry, who were allowed to make improvements or repairs to public property, and then come around afterwards, without the slightest prior justification from this House authorizing the expenditure, and expect this House to repay them. This is done so irregularly, Mr. Chairman, that there is not even an order in council. I wonder if there is any correspon-
[Air. J. H. King.]
dence in connection with this matter? The very least we can have is the production of all the correspondence which has anything whatever to do with this very extraordinary item.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
There is nothing very extraordinary about it. I have tried to give a review of the facts very simply and very plainly. Owing to the fact that the ballast had considerably settled and that the earth surface had been partly washed by the waves, the wharf had become impassable, and in order to render it useful it was necessary to add some ballast stone, about 1,000 cubic yards, and to replace the earth surface by a wooden flooring.
Regarding the commercial necessity for this work, it is reported to me that the farmers and lumbermen of the locality were waiting for these repairs to the wharf to be effected to load and ship about 5,000 cords of pulp-wood, and the Paint River Oxide Company were ready to ship, as soon as the wharf was made passable, from 5,000 to 6,000 tons of their ore in crude state. There was no appropriation for this work, and as the amount was too large to charge against the general appropriation the engineering department recommended that the Paint River Oxide Company be requested to make repairs under the supervision of the district engineer, provided the}^ were willing to wait until a vote to recoup them was passed by parliament. The company have taken that chance, but if parliament does not see fit to recoup them for the expenditure which they properly made in order that they might carry on their business on property owned by the government, there is no objection to cutting the item out; but to say that there have been any backdoor methods whatever in bringing this vote before parliament is unfair. The item is here for discussion. As I have already stated it was too large a sum to take from our general vote; we do not spend large sums from that vote. Here was a company proposing to get their products to the market. They were informed that we had no item in our estimates for the facilities required. It was only natural for the company then to say: It is your property and we will do the work under your supervision if you will pass a vote in parliament to recoup us for the expenditure. That is all there is in the transaction.

Has my hon.
friend anything showing the undertaking of the government to do this? How did the government come to undertake it?

Supply-Public Works
.Mr. KING (Kootenay):	On the advice of
the chief engineer.

What was the
form of the undertaking in connection with this expenditure?

The department
agreed with the company that if they would carry out the work under our supervision and control we would submit a vote to parliament in the belief that parliament would vote the money.

Has my hon.
friend the agreement with him?

It was done on

Will my hon.

When was the work
finished?

know. I imagine it was within a few weeks.

May I ask the minister
how long previous to that there had been any expenditure of money on this wharf?

Does anybody else use

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs

Item stands.
Pointe au Pic (Murray Bay)-wharf repairs, $9,000.

speechtext: What county is this in?

speechtext:
Charlevoix-
Saguenay.

This is for a wharf down
in Murray Bay?

speechtext:
Yes. It is to
repair the damage done to the west side of the wharf by storm in 1924. This is an important port in Murray Bay.

You had $15,000 in the
estimates last year.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes. We spent
When was that spent?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It was spent last year, in 1925-26.
Will the $9,000 complete the work?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes. There is a re-vote of $1,000.
What was the original estimate of the cost of this work?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The structure is
a large one and repairs have been made to it from year to year; it is one of the largest wharves on the St. Lawrence. The total expenditure on it up to March, 1925, was $139,000.

This expenditure is
amply justified. This is one of the largest ports below Quebec. I think the leader of the opposition has been there and has seen the place. I remember one occasion when he happened to be there and observed the activities which were going on. There will be a good return for every dollar spent. The government receives wharfage dues, and there is a considerable export of pulpwood and other products. The vessels of the Canada Steamship line call at the port daily.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I was not disputing the
necessity of keeping up the wharf there. I just marvelled though that the government would buy another wharf for $18,000 in the hon. member's county, especially one that is no good, and then pay the people from whom they bought it seven thousand more to put it in shape for their own use.
I do not know anything about it.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
That is what I marvel
at. I hope the hon. member has not neglected the rest of his riding in the same way.
I am not neglecting my riding. I am talking about the part with which I am more familiar. I do not happen to know this part as well.

We accept my
hon. friend's alibi in connection with that, but he scented the trouble at once and he was taking to cover.

Hon. members should
not put into my mouth things I did not say. I am not taking to cover, but I do not want to be held responsible before the House and the country for recommending something I do not know anything about.

When was the contract let?

speechtext:
An order in
council was passed last year in August and this is to complete the work. A new contract is being let for this work.
Was any money spent last year and if so, how much?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I am sorry I have not the information of the amount of work done last year.

Did the minister have a
vote for similar work last year?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
How much was the vote?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I understand
from my deputy that the money that was expended was from the general vote last year.
What general vote?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The dredging vote for Ontario and Quebec.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: A general vote was used to start a work which now requires a special vote of $54,000? The order in council I understand was passed in the month of August of last year. Was this order in. council, under which the government without any authority from parliament commenced at that point work which is committing the country to an expenditure for which we have an item of $54,000, passed about the same date as that of the Richmond Hill speech?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
My right hon. friend is entirely mistaken. It is just as well to forget the election of last year. This had nothing to do with it. This is an important point on the St. Lawrence river and it is very necessary that this work should be done. It is an important lumbering point. The exports consist of about [DOT] 15,000,000 feet B.M. of lumber, 9,000 cords of pulpwood,
8,000	cords of slab and 3,000,000 feet of laths. The total tonnage of general merchandise of all kinds exported is about 20,000 tons, consisting of hay, cheese, butter, honey, raw hides, meat, cattle, maple sugar, manufactured products, etc. The St. Lawrence Paper Mills are operating at that point. As regards taking money from the general vote for this work, there is nothing unusual in that.
Just a moment ago the minister told us that he had an order in council covering the work of last year. Will he give us the date?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The order in
council of last year was passed on the 20th August, 1925, granting authority to accept the tender of the National Dock and Dredging Company of Quebec. They did not finish their contract. I have not the amount of work they did. They were in there until November.
What date was the contract let?

speechtext:
The order in
council was passed in August.

Mr. -KING (Kootenay):	That was the
