speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I have no objection.

I am not speaking about the merits of the work because I do not know anything about it; but this is another case where we have an extraordinary departure from ordinary principles and it is absolutely necessary to have the order in council produced. This is a departure from ordinary principles because the memory of this committee is not so short as not to recollect the statement of the minister in connection with a paint company; it was to be left to look after repairs amounting to $7,000 in connection with a public wharf because the item was too big. At the same time we have the statement made that the same vote, the genera! vote, is made use of for the purpose of supporting a liability of $26,000. This is new. The minister shakes his head. There is no question about the facts. Unless my hon.- friend is entirely mistaken in what he has told the committee, the usual rule which is well known is that a new contract cannot and ought not to be entered into until this House has first supplied funds for the purpose of carrying out that contract. One of the first things the Auditor General has to see is the certificate of the vote and all that sort of thing. All that is forgotten for some reason which perhaps we shall be able to get from the order in council. In connection with this contract it was necessary to disregard all the usual safeguards with which the public treasury is surrounded. The minister ought to bring down not only the order in council 
but all other papers having regard to this particular transaction, correspondence and so on, particulars as to when the work started, how much was paid last year and the like.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: There is no objection at all to bringing down the order in council and other information. This is a natural transaction in the department. Riviere du Loup is an important point. In order that navigation might be proceeded with at that point the department entered into a contract for certain dredging. It is hoped to complete the work this year and we are asking parliament for a certain sum.

I know something about the locality having visited it. Where is the dredging being done? The wharf at Riviere du Loup is a very fine one extending away out into the St. Lawrence. Is the dredging at the wharf or up the river?

Last year a contract was
let for the dredging of about 50,000 cubic yards but the contractor did not complete the work. On October 15, I believe, the Tourville Lumber Company was sold to the St. Lawrence Lumber Company and I ascertained in an interview with one of the proprietors of the Tourville concern that the St. Lawrence company had asked for more dredging to be done because they intended operating on a larger scale. I suppose the contract has been increased owing to the demand of the company for greater accommodation. There is regular steamship communication between Montreal, Berthier and Louiseville twice a week and all the traffic, which is considerable, is carried by water. I have received correspondence in connection with the subject and I can assure the committee that the dredging is necessary.

The committee
will be grateful for the information the hon. member has volunteered. I observe his activity in the matter and he is no doubt gratified at the success of his efforts. I have no doubt he will produce this evening the correspondence to which he has referred.

The company asked for
further dredging in view of the fact that they intended operating on a larger scale the business taken over from the Tourville Lumber Company, and1 the facts are all set out in the correspondence that passed between the business men interested in the matter, the St. Lawrence and the Tourville Companies, and myself. I know nothing about the order

Supply-Public Works
in council, but I will allow the hon. gentleman to look into this private correspondence if he cares to do so. The oiption was accepted on October 15 last and the dredging was begun during the month of November.

I do not think
the hon. gentleman is a bit ashamed of the correspondence, but I can see that some of his friends are afraid of it They do not want it produced; they regard it as something in the nature of gunpowder.
Oh, oh.

Hon. gentlemen roar at the suggestion that the correspondence be produced, but surely there is nothing private about public business, and any representations made to the minister should be open to parliament. The house has a right to know on what grounds the member for the district was able to arrange this matter. If the hon. member (Mr. Ger-vais) does not want to produce the correspondence dealing with the subject-it is not private correspondence-that is a matter for himself, and I shall be content to accept his refusal. However, I think he has a better appreciation of his position and of the duty he owes the public than have some of his friends.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the item carry?
No, the item is not carried.
Carried.

Notwithstanding insistent shouts of "carried" from hon. gentlemen from Quebec, the item is not going through at present. We can discuss it all over again if hon. gentlemen are so ignorant of the proper, legal, honest way of carrying on the business of the country as to rush through an item of this kind before the committee has been given adequate information regarding it. It seems to me the course of action in this case has been extraordinary. I need hardly observe that it is one of the principles of our form of government that no public funds shall be spent, nor shall any credit be extended, except by a vote of the House. I am sure hon. gentlemen, bearing that in mind, will refrain, from shouts of "carried" when they discover that a contract for $26,000 was let without the attention of parliament being called to the matter. This is something that calls for an explanation. Surely hon. gentlemen opposite will demand that explanation. Or are they so convinced
that the whole thing has been improperly carried out that it will not stand ventilation? If that is their fear they will again call "carried", but if they think that parliament has a right to get at the facts they will demand that an explanation be given.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I take exception
to that statement. It is all right for my hon. friend to fill Hansard with that kind of material, but nothing has been done in this matter contrary to the usual practice that has always obtained in the department.
You are wrong.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: We vote certain sums of money every year for dredging in the Maritime provinces, in Quebec, in Ontario and elsewhere and contracts are let for certain work. These contracts are advertised in the pulblic press and tenders are received; the matter then goes before council and the contract is awarded. Why make any mystery out of it?

Is the contract let before
parliament passes upon it?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
No; we vote so
much money for dredging in the different provinces and the work is carried on in this way.

The minister
knows that usually the dredging is done by the government's own fleet.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Some of it; not all.

Oh no, not all. But the minister also knows that all contracts of over $5,000 are submitted to parliament; that is, if the proper and the usual procedure is followed. My hon. friend shakes his head. If my hon. friend would only be consistent I at least would be able to understand him a great deal better. Take the example we have had already this afternoon We have the statement made by the hon. minister that the general vote which the department has to look after small matters would not justify the expenditure on the paint company's wharf of $7,000, and yet at the same time we have the same minister saying it is perfectly proper and usual to take the general vote to support a contract of $26,000.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
My hon. friend
is trying to confuse two votes that are treated entirely different in practice, and he well knows it. The general dredging vote running into hundreds of thousands of dollars is used

Supply-Public Works

by the department to do dredging where necessary, and it must act within the vote and by order in council. There is no mystery aibout this; my hon. friend can have all the correspondence relating to it. It is not unusual, it is done from year to year, and the two items are not to be confused.

Mr. Chairman,
the only reason I am challenging the minister is that his supporters want to carry this vote now.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I am in no hurry about carrying it.
Sir HENRY'DRAYTON: Very well, let it stand.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
My hon. friend
referred to the construction of the paint company's wharf. We did not take the amount from the general vote, thinking it would be fairer and better to bring it before parliament and make the explanation here. That is why the item is in the estimates. So far as the dredging vote is concerned, if my hon. friend wants it to stand over it can. I am sure he will be satisfied when he sees the correspondence.

My recollection is, but I
am subject to correction, that in previous discussions of this sort it has been understood that the general vote is supposed to ibe for amounts up to $2,500, that is, for small repairs. I think the minister said that a year or two ago.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No.

Then how high can the
minister go? Could he spend the whole general vote for Ontario and Quebec on one job without the authority of this parliament?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The practice has been to let contracts from time to time under that vote. It is true the vote is primarily for the maintenance of our own dredging fleet, but in addition to that contracts have for many years been let from that vote. The authority is by order in council, after calling for tenders in the regular and usual way.

Supposing in that way a
contract was let for $75,000 or $100,000, and the House subsequently turned it down, what would happen? Are such contracts let subject to approval by parliament?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The vote is
passed before the contract is let, and was in this case.
The general vote was?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes; and that is where it is paid from.
What was voted for dredging for Quebec and Ontario last year?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Last year we voted $652,000.

What is the amount this
year?

Mr. Chairman, the channel at Riviere du Loup leading to the main channel has not been dredged for several years and the silt brought down by the river has made the channel so shallow that navigation is impeded. I received letters from the officials of the Tourville Lumber Company, which has sold its interests to another company. I know none of the officials of this new company, nor have they asked me to intervene. Three years ago the proprietor of the steamboat plying between Montreal, Berthierville and Louiseville asked me to have this dredging done, as did those interested in the Soulanges steamboats. Last fall they repeated their request because during August and September the boat service could not be maintained owing to the shallowness of the channel, I think the dredging is quite necessary.

I would hasten
to assure the hon. member that I am quite certain of his good faith in this matter. I am not challenging at the moment the necessity for the work, as I said in the first instance, I am trying to find out why we have departed from the usual practice.

Is the minister prepared
to let the item stand until we get more information?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I have no objection.

Mr. Chairman, I shall
have to tell my electors that the dredging was blocked by the other side simply because of a legal distinction. I will tell them exactly what has happened.

Mr. Chairman,
I would tell my hon. friend that despite his terrible threat we are only trying to see that the right thing is done by the people of the country generally; that is, that the public funds are properly conserved, irrespective of

what may happen to anyone. I am sure that when my hon. friend considers what he has said he will temper the wind to the shorn lamb and not be unduly severe.

item. What is the necessity for this expenditure?

I wish to say with
reference to this item, that a large dam was built on Isle Maligne, so that the level of the water could be kept high, in order that people would be able to navigate around the lake. Formerly during summer time the water was rather low, but now, on account of that huge dam that has been built, the water will be kept high,' ensuring navigation during the season. The Price Company has a large paper mill built at River Bend and they have to use two large tugs to bring their pulpwood from the Mistassini river down to River Bend, I think they built some kind of dry dock, especially for the repair of their tugs, and this wharf will be very convenient for them. It is absolutely necessary.

item at a point like that.

The department

Trois-Rivieres-repairs to coal dock, $4,950.

I wonder why that comes in here, Mr. Chairman. We passed an act last year, or the year before, transferring these properties to the harbour commission. We understood that the harbour commission was going to run all these properties, and that the department would be out of it. I understand that the harbour commission is functioning at Three Rivers.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: This is a structure owned by the people of Canada. The work consists of repairing with concrete the inclined ice breaker situated along the upstream side of the wharf, and most urgent repairs to the wooden sheeting of the wharf. The engineer reports that the ice breaker is all rotten and decayed, and if not repaired a part of the structure may be carried away and the coal elevators put in danger. There is a considerable traffic on this coal wharf. In 1925, up to November, 27 steamers loaded with coal, pig iron, rails, angle bars, fish plates, and so forth, landed at this wharf with cargoes representing 145,543 tons. It is true that the harbour commission had a bill passed last year, but there was no money granted by that bill, and we have transferred none of our property to the harbour commission. The Marine department are in control of this wharf, and are charging fees for its use. This appropriation is required to maintain the wharf.

That is an extraordinary thing, because we were told in this House during this session in connection with the Chicoutimi harbour commission that the Three Rivers harbour commision was functioning very well, with no trouble. My hon. friend now says that it is not functioning at all, that the Marine department are looking after the harbour, and that there is no money for the harbour commission to carry on with. Who is collecting the fees?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: This wharf is administered by the Marine department. It is our property, not the property of the harbour commission. There has been no transfer of property, and we are maintaining a public wharf there. I do not think there has been any suggestion that we should turn this wharf over to the harbour commission. It is true that, the harbour commission is functioning and collecting revenue, but not from this structure.

What property has been transfered to the commission?

The largest on lake

This is required for general repairs and improvements to harbour and river works in Ontario. Seven items have been noted by the engineering department for expenditures this year and, as I have explained before, this amount is

speechtext:

speechtext: I have no allotment for Belle River.

There is at Kenora an important wharf that requires limited but very necessary improvement, particularly at this season of the year. There is going to be an international regatta there for one thing, and more than that, a good deal of shipping passes over the wharf. It was built some years ago, but it stands in need of considerable improvement to-day. I would ask the minister to look into the matter with a view to making such improvements as are found necessary.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I shall be glad to consider the matter.

The committee will be pained to hear the minister's reply to my hon. friend (Mr. Robinson) who has called attention to the sad state of affairs at Belle River. Some time ago the great importance of that harbour was impressed upon us: a large sum of money had to be spent at Belle River; we had to have a wharf there and it was absolutely imperative to do dredging and more dredging and still more dredging. Now, what has happened to Belle River? We are told to-night that although the wharf is finished the channel is now silted up and yet nothing is to be done about it. I am told by an hon. gentleman that it is partly broken down. Is nothing to be done for it? Or has the department now joined the "dry" forces as against the "wet" forces? I think the House knew very well

that this wharf was very convenient for a particular traffic that certain gentlemen were supposed to be interested in. My hon. friend remembers that immortal bit of poetry, how Tim needed' King and King needed Tim? Now that Tim is no longer with us, has the usefulness of this port entirely ceased? Are we to say "amen" to all further expenditures at Belle River? Silted up-partly broken down-nothing for it in the estimates-Tim gone. Is that the trouble? [DOT]

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Not at all. We
undertook certain developments at Belle River on the advice of the engineering department. It was suggested that another revetment wall should be .built to confine the waters and prevent the silting up of the channel. I have not consented to that additional expenditure, and that is why there is no item for it in the estimates.
My hon. friend finds himself suddenly filled with righteous resolution in connection with this matter.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Oh no.

He has got
his back to the wall, he is going to stop any further expenditure at Belle River. Will he go further and tell us-as the fact is-that he looks upon the money already spent there as thrown away? We have spent now well over $100,000 there, according 'to my recollection, with which I think the minister will agree. The channel has silted up just as we said it would. I do not know whether the wharf is used now or not. I want to go into a little bit of history in that connection. I am not suggesting for one minute that the minister knew where he was going to be led, but I recall on the first vote-and we debated it a good deal.-my hon. friend's information was that $30,000 would be the whole bill. It was not going to take very much the first year, but the expenditure went up and up until it was well over $100,000. Now, is that all to be abandoned, or is the channel again to be dredged? If so, for What?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
My hon. friend
is entirely mistaken. It is true that for many years money has been spent at Belle River for dredging, not only by this administration but by its predecessors. When my hon. friend says $100,000, he means the expenditure by his government.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: We spent a certain sum of money to try to correct the silted condition of the channel.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Will the minister siana
up and say that he spent only $20,000?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I am speaking for this government.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: No, his own government has spent hundreds of thousands of dollars there.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
No. Before the
Public Accounts committee last session the evidence was not by any means what my hon. friends desired to bring out. The expenditure at Belle River was undertaken on the recommendation of the department-
Of Tim Healy.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: -it being suggested that once we built a retaining wall probably it would be necessary to build a second retaining wall. From the information I have received, if the work is to be effective probably another retaining wall will have to be built, but I am not satisfied that conditions warrant this further expenditure.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
We will get the details
shortly. The hon. minister knows his government has spent hugely larger sums than he states.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I do not think
so.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Yes he has, and we will be able to demonstrate it. The government did it in pursuance of a fraudulent election pledge.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Yes, nothing else. I was in the contest and I know-I saw the pledge.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman,
there was no fraudulent election pledge at all.

King does not need
Tim.
Not now.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The late Mr. Kennedy was elected in 1921, and as a member of this House and a minister of the crown he recommended to the government that this work be done. It was under consideration and being developed when he died.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Being developed?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Yes.
Supply-Public Works

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Not at all. I would
do more honour to the memory of the late Mr. Kennedy than to say of him what the minister says. It is true the late Mr. Kennedy had it under consideration, which means that some constituents were pressing it upon him, but never did it come to any maturity until the by-election in the month of March, 1923. Then in order to elect the government candidate, although at the general election they had a seven thousand majority, this government, through their agents, scattered throughout the riding handbills promising all sorts of public works. Those handbills were scattered up and down the riding by the thousand promising to bribe the electors with the money of the people of Canada. One of those handbills was produced in this House, and I have it yet. It ran something like this:
King needs Tim; so do you.
Tim and King-that is the thing.
King and Tim were to be paid for out of the treasury, and the new Minister of Public Works was to be made the agent for the purpose. He made himself the agent, he put a vote in the estimates the first year in the neighbourhood of $30,000, and he built something at Belle River. But from the hour he started to build until now there has never been anything come to that wharf save a few gasoline launches to bootleg whisky into the United States. There never was any other purpose for it. The minister poured money by the tens of thousands of dollars into that wharf, and he would not be a whit more guilty to-day if he had stood with his friend Tim Healy at Belle River and thrown it dollar by dollar into the water.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I take exception
to my right hon. friend's statement. The undertakings of the government were properly undertaken. It is not so.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: What is not so?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That we threw
away tens of thousands of dollars.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Certainly. The minister
himself says he spent $20,000.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Will my hon.
friend say his government did not spend any money at Belle River?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Certainly, we spent
money everywhere, but never for the purpose of-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
For the purpose
of shipping in and out of Belle River.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The money spent before 1923-
I rise to a point of order, Mr. Chairman. What item are we discussing?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The general estimates.
Let me tell the hon. member for Missisquoi that I am glad he has had some sleep; he worked so hard that he was entitled to it. The money spent in Belle River prior to 1923 was a bagatelle, amounting to nothing; but this government has thrown money away there by the tens of thousands of dollars, and stands to-day convicted of having squandered it on a worthless enterprise for nothing but political purpose, as a bribe to the voters- an enterprise that the government now abandons. The minister stands up and says that to make it any good they have to spend more money on it but he is not going to consent to any further expenditure. The fact of the matter is that expenditure served its purpose. Now the money the people have paid out of their earnings, the taxes, the whole thing is wasted, and the government is convicted of a fraud.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it
would1 be well for the members of the House to read the reports of the Public Accounts committee which investigated this matter last session. The evidence then presented showed that due to- the work that had been carried on by this government there had been stimulated in that district a brick plant and other developments. Money has been spent at Belle River for the last fifty years.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
What are the "other
developments"?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I have not the
particulars before me.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Was the minister ever
there?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I should think not.

Would
the minister give us the amount spent at Belle River last year, the year before and the year before that again?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Belle River is not under discussion. If my hon. friend wishes the information I shall be very glad to have the question asked and reply to it.

My hon. friend is not
fair to the committee in that statement. When estimates of this kind are before the

Supply-Public Works
467:
House the minister invariably has his deputy with him, as is the case to-night, and it is quite customary for the deputy to bring with him all the figures affecting matters of this kind. We have discussed this subject every session. It is a matter upon which hon. members on this side have taken a very strong stand, warning the minister as to the inadvisability of this work right from its very inception; and it is a subject that the minister must have expected or known would arise. I submit that it is not fair to ask that members place the question on the order paper and then await the chance of an answer. We are entitled to an answer now.

There is no item for Belle River this year, and we can hardly expect the minister to furnish information as to amounts spent in the last three or four or five years, or an item which does not exist so far as this year is concerned. We might as well bring down information as to money spent twenty years ago. The minister could not be expected to bring down everything spent in the department for twenty years.

My hon. friend has not
grasped the point. We are considering item 147, which involves an expenditure of $773,000. It may be that no specific detail is mentioned regarding this, but it is reasonable to expect the minister to have it. If the minister has not the information under his hand, he can let the item stand and bring it down.

But there is no item to
stand.

The whole item can
stand.

The whole of the Ontario
item?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The theory of the hon.
member (Mr. Power) is that if the government abandons a worthless project it never can be criticized for what it did in reference to it.

No, my hon. friend is
wrong. I do not think my hon. friend (Mr. Stevens) is serious when he criticizes the minister for not having before him estimates with regard to Belle River when no question regarding Belle River is before the House.

No, I am not criticizing
him for that. But I criticize him for saying "Put the question on the order paper and I
will answer it." When the minister is asked for reasonable information in regard to the works in this or any other part of the country, the House is entitled to that information.

The hon. member thinks
the minister should have it with him.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The hon. member for Vancouver Centre must have misunderstood me. I said that the item for Belle River was not in the estimates, and that I had not the information here. I shall be glad to supply that information to the committee.
That is all right.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Or I shall be
glad to answer questions on the order paper. Many questions have been put to the government, but there was no question about Belle River. Belle River was investigated by the Public Accounts committee last year. I shall see that the information is furnished.
To the committee?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I can furnish a little information now that will perhaps help the minister. He said that this government spent $20,000 in all. I may say that he spent $29,000 odd in 1934 alone. I have the item before me. It appears in the Public Accounts for 1924 at page part V-106:

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Midland, in the township of Tay, county of Simcoe, is a thriving port, situated at the southeasterly extremity of the Georgian bay, and has a population of 8,400. The town is a terminus of the Canadian National railway, distant 102 miles from Toronto, and is 9 miles by water from the Georgian bay port of the Canadian Pacific railway, namely, Port McNichol. The town is primarily a marine centre and its chief business water-borne commerce. Its industries are as follows:	Grain elevators-five
houses in operation having a total 9 p.m. capacity of 8,500,000 bushels, and a sixth house under construction,
1,500,000	bushels capacity. There are two saw mills and three flour mills with a capacity of 1,200 barrels per day, and coal docks. The Midland Shipbuilding Company is located there. The largest ship constructed to date is the Glenifer, 560 feet long. Other concerns are the Georgian Bay Shipbuilding and Wrecking Company, the International Fibre Board Company, the Midland Wood products Company, the Midland Boat Works, Machine and Foundry Shop, and others. It is quite an extensive industrial town and the port is considered one of the best on the upper lakes.

I am indebted to the minister for the information he has given; I am very glad to have it. We in the west are very much interested in the port of Midland, and I hope the minister will continue to give it any legitimate assistance it may require. The port is of great value to western Canada.

That is too slow a rate of progress. The harbour is badly needed in Oshawa.
What do you want a harbour for?

Why do we need a harbour? If you close Oshawa harbour you might just as well close all the harbours along the lake. I wish to say to hon. members that at Oshawa we take in more tonnage than all the ports between Montreal and Toronto put together, and we should like to be able to use that harbour to a still greater extent. Some of our manufacturers have already secured sites along the Lachine canal in Montreal for the storage of their goods. It has been anticipated for some time that they will be able to use the Oshawa harbour to ship goods in that way. We started out to have a harbour there. The old harbour was destroyed. They went to work to reconstruct and rebuild it and we had hopes that in five years' time we would have our harbour, but with this tremendously reduced appropriation the period of its completion will be postponed almost indefinitely. The reduction means that the work will go on a little too slowly. We do not wish the full amount voted at once, but we think that within four or five years we are entitled to have a harbour at Oshawa, and the government should give the matter a little more consideration.

other day from the secretary-treasurer of the municipality of East St. Paul's, which is north of Winnipeg. The conditions complained of in the resolution are also to be found at many points along the Red river between Winnipeg and St. Andrew's locks on both banks, and matters are getting gradually worse. I have directed the attention of the department to this state of affairs on several occasions, but so far little has been done. Some work has been performed in the shape of riprap in connection with St. Andrew's locks, and I have no doubt that the department fully realize that the construction of those locks has been responsible for the erosion along the banks of Red river even further south than Winnipeg. The resolution in question is accompanied by a letter which reads:
At the last meeting of council-
That is, the council of St. Paul's:
-a delegation of ratepayers waited on the council re the erosion of the banks of the Red river especially as it affects lots 88, 89 and 90 and the following resolution was passed.
The resolution is to the effect that a letter be written to the chief engineer at Winnipeg and to the mentbers representing the different constituencies, bringing the matter to their attention. The letter then states:
The ratepayers living on these banks report that the situation is becoming serious not only to their property but also to the main highway which cornea very close to the banks of the Red river at lots 88 and 89.
I can endorse this resolution because I know that what it states is quite correct. I am familiar with almost every foot of the beach from Winnipeg to lake Winnipeg and I know just what the conditions are like along the river. Before the construction of St. Andrew's lodes the beach along the river to Winnipeg on both sides was stony, and there was absolutely no danger of erosion or of washout while the river was at normal height. But since the raising of the water by the construction of the locks the level has gone beyond the stony beach and consequently the banks along the river, particularly at certain points, are being rapidly washed away, so that the road on each side of the river is being damaged to a considerable extent. I wish to give the minister timely warning, because if this condition is allowed to continue the Dominion government will be responsible for a large sum of money in the shape of damages by the construction of St. Andrew's locks. I should like to see the government take action. This is a question of very great importance to the people of that district, but I do not

Supply-Public Works
wish to take up any further time of the House discussing it; on the contrary, I wish to do all I can to expedite the business of the House, because like many other western members I feel we have been a very long time here and so far as I can see we have accomplished very little in the interests of the country. I repeat, I am anxious to expedite the business of the House so that we may be able to get home as soon as possible. I do not mean to say that we should overlook any questions of importance, but during the six months we have been here we have wasted far too much time, and I certainly want to see the remaining business disposed of without further delay.
I want to ask the hon. minister another question. We have been working on the harbour at Big George's island, lake Winnipeg, for about six years. Will any portion of the item we are now voting or of the general item under dredging be devoted towards the completion of this harbour?

Then again the vote of $10,000 for harbours and rivers generally is far below what is necessary to meet our requirements. We have a harbour commission at Winnipeg, and as a result of the development of St. Andrew's locks a few years ago there is a good deal of tonnage coming up and down the river, necessitating a harbour of some kind. The absence of proper accommodation is a very great handicap to the development of Winnipeg, a city of 250,000 people. I am sure if the minister looks into the matter he will have no hesitation in making provision for improving the semblance of a wharf that we have there now. I hope when the supplementary estimates come down we shall find he has inserted at least $50,000 for this purpose. I am confident I can convince the minister of the pressing necessity for improving the wharf to such an extent that it will meet the requirements of the traffic that has developed there. I am glad to see an item for Victoria Beach, but it is too small. Last year the vote was $24,000. Has that been spent?

In proof of that I may say that no money has been spent on account of any erosion of banks taking place north of St. Andrew's locks, between St. Andrew's locks and lake Winnipeg, a distance of something like thirty miles. When the water is at its normal height all 
the year round no erosion takes place; the banks are protected by the natural stony beach. But when the water has been raised by reason of construction to twenty feet above normal you can readily understand that there is no protection afforded by the stony beach, because the water is lapping on the shore above. That is why the erosions take place. I do not know what the report of the engineer is, and I do not care. The matter is becoming serious, and the government must do something to protect certain points along the river. They have done so to some extent already. WTien the government built the St. Andrew's locks they realized that erosion would take place along the river and they made provision to protect the bank at many points by riprapping the stone. These points therefore are guarded, but there is erosion at other points not protected. The condition is getting worse every year; as much as thirty feet of roadway have been washed out through the parish of St. Andrew's north of Winnipeg. I hope the government will put something in the supplementary estimates to prevent the . erosion taking place along the river.

It is up to this government or to any government to meet the conditions which have been brought about by this lowering of the water level. To what extent the Chicago diversion is responsible I am not prepared to say, but it is the duty of this government or of any other government to meet the situation fairly, and so far as I am concerned, speaking from this side of the House, I am prepared to give very generous consideration to supplementary estimates brought in with the intention of meeting those changed conditions.

speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Esquimalt-old dry dock-to provide for payment of repairs performed by Messrs. P. Lyall and Sons Construction Company, Limited, with interest thereon at 5 per cent, $5,262.84.
What is the idea of the interest there?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
This amount had
been earned on October 1, 1924. The cost of the work was $4,895.67. The interest from October 1, 1924 to March 31, 1926 is $367.17 making a total of $5,262.84.
What was the reason for the delay in payment? As a general rule interest is never allowed on government payments, as my hon. friend knows.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I think what happened was this: A ship was being built in the old dry dock in Victoria. She came into contact with the walls and there was certain damage. An arrangement was made with the P. Lyall Company to repair this damage, and this is an adjustment of that account.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Edgewood wharf-repairs, $4,200.
Where is Edge-wood?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It is on the Arrow lakes in the constituency of West Kootenay. This is to renew the superstructure of the wharf.
That will be a new contract.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: New work.
It has not been let yet.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
False creek-dredging, $50,000.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: This is for the removal of 121,790 cubic yards of sand, silt, debris and gravel in False creek. False creek, as my hon. friend knows, is in the centre of the city of Vancouver and many industries are located on its banks. It is proposed by means of this dredging to give access to those manufacturing properties in order that there may be protection in case of fire and also that they may have ingress or egress from or to the harbour.

Have we still
the title, or is it in the hands of the provincial government?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The harbour commission are in control, but I think there has been certain litigation that would indicate
Supply-Public Works

that the ownership is in the provincial government. The hon. member for Burrard, who is in his seat, would probably be more familiar with recent litigation and the decision of the court than I.

I do not think there is any litigation. I believe the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) could throw more light on the matter if he were in his seat. I think there has been a settlement as between the federal and provincial governments and the right to the harbour as regards False creek has been handed over to the province in return for other concessions.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Not handed over to the province.
The industrial island is certainly handed over to the province.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: They are not collecting any rentals; those are collected by the harbour board and under their administration, I understand.

The minister should certainly know the present position of the matter, but an agreement was announced by the Minister of Justice, I think, two years ago in this House. The harbour board may still be administering it on behalf of the provincial authorities.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I think we have an arrangement with the provincial government whereby they continue to be in control and administer it and collect the rentals. The provincial government are not asserting their right.
But the title is in the provincial government?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

And it is administered by
the harbour board on their behalf?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Fraser river-improvements, $50,000.

Has the minister included in this item 13,000 for protection work south of the ferry landing at Rosedale? This matter was taken up by the late member in 1924, and the federal government promised the expenditure, the provincial and municipal authorities to provide a similar amount. Is that provided for in this estimate?
[Mr. J. H. King.)

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Not in this estimate. There has been co-operation between the provincial government and the municipality, and I hope that parliament will later on supplement the Dominion contribution to the work.

The work is completed.
The provincial government have paid their portion and the municipality has borne its share of the cost as well as that of the Dominion government. There is a matter of $1,000 for a wing dam across the river at Agassiz, and I have a letter from the municipality of the district of Kent in which it is stated that the provincial government has agreed to grant $1,000 and the municipality another $1,000. They have appealed to the Dominion government for its contribution of an equal amount for the work across the river.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
There is no commitment on the part of the Dominion government, but we shall be glad to look into the matter and decide whether -we are involved and how much we should contribute.
Mr. ftARBER:	I understand that the attention of the department has been called to the fact that the Canadian Pacific Railway has dumped several trainloads of rock into the bed of the Fraser at Mission to strengthen a bridge at that point. This intereferes with navigation at certain seasons. What will be done to rectify it?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I cannot recall
having had the matter brought to my attention. I shall be glad to make inquiries.

The suggestion was made
that it might be better, instead of compelling the Canadian Pacific to remove the rocks, to negotiate with them with a view to having the bridge used for general traffic as well as for the purposes of the railway.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That suggestion
has been considered, but there is not much likelihood of the company agreeing to the proposal. They state that the bridge is not capable of bearing the added traffic.

What is being done
with regard to Woodward slough?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The money is required to carry out the work which was under construction last year at Woodward slough to control the river at that point, and also to deepen the channel.

Supply

Public Works

What is the minimum depth of the channel at high tide between
New Westminster and the gulf?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Between twentyseven and twenty-nine feet.

Is twenty-seven the
minimum?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
At what point?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
At Woodward
slough and near the entrance to the Fraser.
What depth will be attained as a result of operations?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
It is difficult to
say, but we hope to improve the channel so that there will be a depth of twenty-nine or thirty feet. It might go more than that, but that is what we hope to reach at any rate.
Your objective is thirty feet?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

Will there be a depth
of thirty feet to the gulf?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes, if some other spot does not fill up.
But assuming that the other points remain as they are now?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: There will be thirty feet.

These are the only
places where you do not reach that depth?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
There are two
important points, one at the mouth of the river, which has been under control in the last two or three years, although there has been some difficulty this winter, and the other at King Edward cut. There is also a section near New Westminster where a wing-dam has been put in and where some money will have to be spent. At present there .is no serious difficulty there, but that part of the river is also under observation. There are these three points to be taken care of.
Is the department doing anything in connection with these three places?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
They are not provided for in this vote.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
This vote will
continue the work undertaken last year at Woodward slough, which is of importance, but other sections of the river are also under consideration.
But it is not included in this vote?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No.

Is the department
considering an extension to the jetty at the mouth of the Fraser river out to deep water?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

Will that be attended
to this year?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I could not say.

I believe the minister
has received representations from the harbour board and others in New Westminster, pointing out the necessity for immediate action in this connection. Are those representations receiving consideration?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

The minister knows,
of course, that there has been a very considerable increase in deep sea shipping at the port of New Westminster in recent years, and he knows also that great industrial development is taking place along the Fraser river.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

Has he any details in
regard to the shipping on the Fraser river,
in the last year, say?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
There has been
an appreciable increase in the shipping from New Westminster down the Fraser river. Last year 150 seagoing vessels took cargo from Westminster. There was a large shipment of lumber from the town as well as an export of ores. In addition to that there was a movement of unfinished lumber products, box shooks, and other more or less manufactured lumber. There has been a marked increase over the last few years.

In those 150 vessels
there were included a number of Canadian merchant marine boats?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

The minister and the
department might show a lit.tle more expedition in connection with the work in the Fraser river channel. I appreciate the fact that the minister and his deputy and the chief engineer realize that the business al-
Supply-Public Works

ready being done and in prospect warrants substantial expenditures in order to provide a proper channel from New Westminster to the gulf. The minister knows that the improvement of this channel does not in any way operate against any other port in British Columbia. There are many miles of industrial sites available along the Fraser river which will have to be used in the very near future, and will be if the channel is made deep enough. At the present time the ships that come into New Westminster are not able to load to full capacity, and this of course prejudices the port to a certain extent. The minister is also aware that the Fraser river has been investigated by those interested in the shipment of grain through Pacific ports. The Saskatchewan Co-operative Company, the Grain Growers' Company, and other large elevator concerns have investigated the Fraser river with a view to locating elevators at or near New Westminster. This would effect a very important saving by the Canadian National Railways, amounting to about $13 a car, as against Burrard inlet at Vancouver. The people of New AVestminster are asking that this work be taken up and handled efficiently and speedily so that the opportunities which are now presenting themselves for the development of the port may be taken advantage of. I do wish to impress upon the minister the necessity of speeding up the work on the Fraser river and finishing the improvement at the mouth of the river, which all authorities agree will tend to increase the depth of water in the harbour and the channel.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Everyone who is familiar with shipping on the Fraser river realizes the advantage of the route. We have been advancing the project under the advice of the technical men of the department, and I am satisfied my hon. friend will agree that a marked improvement has taken place in the river, so much so that the shipping has quadrupled in the last three or four years. The Fraser river needs to be carefully studied before we undertake to control it. If we advance step by step and let the river assist in correcting the channel, I think we shall accomplish more than if we rush in and attempt extensive works involving large expenditures. I heartily endorse the policy of the engineering branch to proceed cautiously.

Is any part of that vote
for the upper Fraser river?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
No. Any requirements for the upper Fraser river, unless mentioned especially, would come out of the general vote for harbours and rivers.
[ Mr. McQuarrie. ]

What about
contracts there?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
This work will
be done under a new contract. The old contract has been closed out. The date of the old contract was October 25 last.

That was nicely
before the election.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
It would not
have any effect on the election.
Of course notl

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Fraser river-Lower-operation of snag boat, $30,000.

The snag boat on the lower Fraser river operates as far as Chiliwack. I would point out to the minister the importance of keeping the river clear of snags and constructing wing dams. These dams do away with considerable dredging, and that is the reason I have urged in connection with the operation of the snag boat the construction also of a wing dam on the Agassiz side. There are already three on the Rose-dale side, and another wing dam on the other side will tend to keep the river in the centre, and thus save the considerable dredging expenses of previous years.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: This vote will be entirely for operating the snag boat. Wing dams would be another item.
Is there anything on the government programme for the north arm of the Fraser river?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I think we have in mind some dredging of the north arm by the departmental dredge. We will come to that shortly.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Fulford Harbour-Wharf repairs, $2,500.
That is a new vote, is it not?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
It is in the
Nanaimo constituency. This is to renew a portion of the wharf approach, the superstructure and the freight shed. It is in the island district between Vancouver and Victoria.
Is any work going on now?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.

Supply-Public Works
Harbours and rivers generally-repairs and improvements, $65,000.

Does this include any
work on the Okanagan river?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The only work we have on the Okanagan river is the maintenance of the dam at Penticton. We spent some money there two years ago, and I do not think there is necessity for further expenditure this year, but if there is it will come out of this vote.
There is an item included in the estimates for the control dam?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I think not.

Is the minister quite
satisfied that the control dam is in a stable condition?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I understand so.
Is anything included there for the clearing of the river north of Stuart lake, connecting Stuart lake with Tacla lake? There was some money spent on that.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I think two years ago.
Is there not a recommendation as to that?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I think there is
a recommendation asking for further expenditures. There is no provision here.

What about Stuart lake
wharf?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I think that was completed last year.

That was Fraser lake. I
am speaking of Stuart lake wharf.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
No, there is no
item after that.	.
You have a requisition for that.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I was thinking
of Fraser lake. I think that was completed last year.	.

Fraser lake wharf was
completed and this is for a similar wharf at Stuart lake further north.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I will make inquiry.
Is a portion of this money to be expended in Victoria harbour?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No, I think some work is to be done in Victoria harbour from our dredging vote or special vote.

Nothing about any work
on Hospital Rock?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: We have it under consideration. It is not in the main estimates.

I might call attention to
the fact that during a foggy day last year one of the big steamers got stuck on that rock.

Is there anything in the
vote in reference to the Coquitlam river? You will remember that this was taken up with the department by the board of trade of Coquitlam in February, 1925. I have a resolution from the board of trade which reads a4 follows:
Copy of a resolution passed by the Port Coquitlam Board of Trade at a meeting held on February 27, 1925.
Whereas the Coquitlam river is a very grave menace in its present state, and whereas the said river has washed away the homes and property of some of our citizens, and whereas the said river is constantly overflowing its banks and spreading over our city, and whereas numerous log jams and bars have formed in the river bed causing the river to keep changing its course;
Be it resolved that this Board of Trade earnestly request the Dominion Government to take such measures as may be necessary to confine the said river to its own channel.
This is a matter I would like to press, and I hope the department has it under consideration. .

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I am familiar
with the Coquitlam river. In 1923-24, in cooperation with the provincial government, we did some work there. I have not been convinced that the Dominion government should spend further money at that point. True, they had bad floods and overflowing of the river some years ago, but I understand the work done in 1923 and 1924 has given great relief, and there has not been any serious damage since.

I understand you have a
vote of $25,000 for the upper Peace river, from Hudson Hope up Peace river. I think the engineer reported that there was to be a vote of that amount included in the estimate.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I do not find it
here.

What is the situation there in regard to the improvement of the Peace
river?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That country is being opened up. Pioneers are going in, and there have been suggestions that we should
Supply-Public Works

provide accommodation that they may be able to get in and out of the district. But there is nothing in these estimates relating to that.

The minister is aware that there is a coal mine operating in there and shipping coal down the river. The capacity of the mine at the present time is 100 tons per day, and during the season of navigation the market is entirely down the river. The river is open for navigation for some 300 miles, except for 15 miles, and I think there are only a few points where work will be required to make the river navigable for the whole distance. A substantial quantity of coal is used by the inhabitants in the district along the river. I understand the matter has been under consideration for the last three years, and promises have been made that attention would be given to it. The people there are anticipating a vote, an appropriation, which I thought would be included in this item. Will the minister put it in the sup-plementaries, or at least give it further consideration?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I shall be glad to give it consideration. When the hon. member spoke of it first I did not think he was referring to Hudson Hope. I am not sure that we have had any direct representations regarding the matter.

The minister has had a
report from Mr. Doncaster.

Another matter taken up with the department some time ago, in regard to which I do not see provision in the estimate, is in relation to the Minnekahda wharf on the Pitt river. This wharf was constructed by the Dominion government and has been repaired from time to time by the municipality. The reason given by the government for not repairing it now is that the municipality during each season unloaded a certain amount of road material there. I believe the department will reconsider their decision not to repair. The wharf is used by a large number of farmers and people of the other districts who do not pay taxes in that municipality, therefore it is unfair to ask the municipality to bear the full cost. This is only a very small amount. It requires some caps and joists in the centre of the wharf where they have been broken. I appeal to the minister to consider this and place an amount in supplementary estimates. As I have said, only a few hundred dollars would be required. Considering the fact that the municipality have from year to year repaired 
the planking and other parts of the wharf, they thought it would not be out of the way to ask the Dominion government to replace the piles and make the necessary repairs.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I think the matter is receiving attention. There is no doubt that the municipality, in the use of the wharf, has overloaded it and done certain damage. The suggestion has been made, I believe, that if the wharf was repaired there should be certain co-operation in the matter.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Port Clements-wharf repairs, $3,000.
Did we not do work there last year?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes, there was a vote there last year of $6,600 and $6,655 was expended.
When was the contract made?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: August 20, 1925.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Saaniohton-renewal of float and wharf repairs,

In connection
with all the items on the rest of the page, no work was done?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I do not think so. There may have been at Saanichton.

The estimate
does not show anything.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
No, there was
nothing.
Nothing in connection with the others, except a report and a speech by the hon. member.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It was reported on.

speechtext:
The next item is:
Harbours and rivers generally, $30,000.
Would the minister give a list of the items under harbours and rivers generally?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is not known yet. These are small items that come up from time to time. This is the item we discussed this afternoon. There is a situation at the city of Prince George in connection with the
Nechacco river in regard to which I think the minister has a certain amount of information. Is he in a position to say whether favourable consideration will be given to an expenditure at that point?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: In connection with the flooding of the river banks at Prince George, there have been requests made to the Public Works department, but I think if my hon. friend will investigate he will find that this is largely a railway matter. Railway lands are involved as well as private property, and as yet we have not seen our way clear to undertake work at that point.

There has been a request made by the navigation companies on the Muskoka lakes for repair of the breakwater at Bracebridge, which has got badly out of repair. Can the minister say whether those repairs will be made this year?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I think that is
being considered.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Item agreed to.

It is getting late, and I think the minister is tired, as we all are. I am sure the Minister of Finance is very anxious to get home, he looks so tired. We have done a good day's work, and I think we can promise the minister that we will do a better day's work to-morrow if he would consent to the committee rising now.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: If it is the desire of the committee, I will move that we rise and report progress.

I was not
present when the items for Prince Edward Island were being passed a few nights ago, and I would like to ask the minister now with respect to the wharf at Georgetown in that province. Strong representations have been made by the Potato Growers' Association at Georgetown with regard to the necessity of frost proofing the warehouse there. This is not an ordinary expenditure. It is an expenditure that would appeal to the people of Prince Edward Island as a whole. Georgetown is the one late port for Prince Edward Island; it is more valuable than any other port for late shipping. The warehouse has been rebuilt at considerable expense during the past two or three years, but it is of very little value, comparatively speaking, unless it is frost proofed. The reason for that is that the growing of seed potatoes is becoming quite a large industry in Prince Edward Island, and a great many of these potatoes go by steamer to the southern United States, where they are re-
Supply -Public Works

quired about the month of January. If we had that warehouse frost proofed it would be possible to load the potatoes on the steamers at Georgetown from two to four weeks later than at any other port in the province. They could go late in December to the southern states and be distributed direct to the growers for seed, thereby saving a great deal of money in the handling. This is a matter of very great importance to the province, and I would ask the minister if he has considered it, and whether there will be an item in the supplementary estimates this year for that purpose.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I am familiar with the situation at Georgetown. The government have reconditioned and renewed a very good wharf at that point, and have improved the shed accommodation. It is true that we have not made that shed frost proof, as I think it should be, for the accommodation of the farmers in the handling of their potatoes, but I would point out that at the present time the railway is on the narrow gauge. We understand that the railway is changing to the broad gauge, and once that is accomplished I think we will be justified in spending some money on a potato warehouse at Georgetown. But until that is done I do not think we would.

That standardization work is going on, and the information we have now is that it will be completed by about September this year. So that if the warehouse is to be made available for shipping this season it would be necessary to have an item in the supplementary estimates this year so that the work could be gone on with now.
There is just one other matter to which I wish to refer, and that is what is known as Lewis point pier at Cardigan. It is the only public wharf in that harbour. Nothing has been done to it for eight or ten years and it has got now into such a state that it is of no value for shipping. There are three private wharves there, but their owners are not keeping them up to any great extent. It is important that the government should consider wharf improvement at that point. This wharf has got into such a bad state of disrepair that it would cost a lot of money to repair it, and my suggestion would be that one of the other private wharves, which are better situated, could be bought Very cheaply, and the Lewis point pier might be removed. One of these other wharves could be obtained for about four or five thousand dollars, possibly less, and it would give all the accommodation required.

I have no doubt that the minister has a report from his engineer on this matter, and I would urge that if at all possible some item be put in the estimates for repairing the present wharf or acquiring one of the others.
Progress reported.
